summary: For ages 9–10, help children use evidence they gather to explain that a moving object has energy (kinetic energy / energy of motion), and that the faster it moves the more energy it has. Keep it strictly qualitative and comparative ('faster → more effect, more energy'): no formulas, no ½mv², no speed or energy measurements. Build the explanation from observed effects (knocks over more, pushes farther, makes a bigger dent/louder bang) while holding the object the same so only speed varies. Name the term precisely and tie it to what children have seen, and separate 'has energy' from 'carries a push' to head off the impetus idea.
misconceptions: 'Only living things / engines have energy' — a rolling ball or blowing wind is not seen as having energy; the damage/movement evidence counters this.
Confusing energy with the force or 'push' the object carries (impetus) — the moving object HAS energy (it can do something), it does not contain a stored push that 'runs out'.
Treating speed and energy as the same thing rather than speed being the EVIDENCE for how much kinetic energy there is.
'A heavier object always has more energy' — mass matters too, but it is deliberately held constant here; don't let it smuggle in (kept for later).
'A stationary object has no energy at all' — it may have stored/potential energy; here we only claim it has no KINETIC energy.

activities.title: Launch-and-hit bench: build the speed→energy explanation from your own trials
steps: Use the SAME ball every time and change only its launch speed (a slider or a fixed ramp released from a low vs high start).

Choose one target (a row of skittles, a loose block, or a sand pit), set it up the same way and in the same place for every trial, fire the ball at it, and record the outcome each trial: how many fell, how far the block moved, how big the dent.
Run several trials ordered slow → medium → fast and lay the outcomes side by side as a results strip.
After a few shots, PREDICT the result of the next speed before firing, then fire to check.
State the explanation in words and point to your evidence: 'the faster it moves, the more energy it has — I know because it knocked over more / pushed it farther.'
Say the term out loud for what the moving ball has: 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion'.
activities.insight: A moving object has kinetic energy; the faster it moves the more energy it has, and comparing the size of the effect on the same target is the evidence for which shot had more energy. Keeping the same object and the same target setup isolates speed as the cause.

activities.title: Swap the evidence: same rule, different effect
steps: Repeat the fast-vs-slow comparison but change what the ball hits: a sand crater to dent, a block to shove, or a buzzer/plate that sounds louder on a harder hit.
For each target, decide which speed produced the bigger effect and say what that tells you about the energy.
Compare across targets: check whether the same rule ('faster → more energy') shows up as more damage, more distance, AND a louder bang in your own results.
activities.insight: The relationship between speed and energy is general: it shows up in many kinds of evidence, not just one toppling task, so the explanation is about the moving object's energy rather than one specific effect.

activities.title: Predict-and-check: ramp roll into dominoes (diagnostic reasoning)
steps: Roll the same object down a ramp from a low start, then from a high start (a higher start, on the same ramp, means it is moving faster at the bottom) into a row of dominoes/blocks.
BEFORE the fast roll, predict how many will move compared with the slow roll, AND say why.
Run the roll and compare your prediction with the result.
Answer the follow-ups: 'It's the same object both times — what does that let you rule out, so what's left?' and 'Where did the fast object's energy go after it hit?'
Consider a still object on the table that knocks nothing down: what does that say about whether a motionless object has kinetic energy?
activities.insight: The reason matters: a speed→energy explanation predicts more effect because faster means more energy; the sameness of the object rules out mass, leaving speed as the cause, and a motionless object has no kinetic energy.

activities.title: Name it and reference it: everyday anchors
steps: Point to everyday cases — a gentle vs hard kick of a football, a slow vs fast bumper car, wind turbines spinning faster in stronger wind — and say which has more energy of motion and how you can tell.
For a labelled picture of a fast cyclist, strong wind, or hard kick, reveal and read the label 'more speed → more energy of motion' to fix the vocabulary.
Use this as a reference to check your words after the hands-on trials, not as a substitute for them.
activities.insight: The term 'kinetic energy' / 'energy of motion' labels something they have observed in the world, not an abstraction detached from evidence.

checkQuestion: You roll the same marble into a line of dominoes twice: once slowly, once fast. The fast marble knocks down far more dominoes. Why does the faster marble knock down more — what's different about it?
checkAnswer: The faster marble has more kinetic energy (energy of motion). The faster something moves, the more energy it carries, so it transfers more energy to the dominoes and knocks more of them down. It's the same marble, so the only difference is speed, and more speed means more energy.
